intents.h2: What do you need help with?
lede: Pick the one that sounds like you. Every route ends in the same place — a quote shopped across the carriers we represent — but the thing to watch out for is different in each case.
Different starting points, same finish: your details in front of several insurance companies at once. What changes is which part of it is worth paying attention to.
Most people arrive here for one of these reasons. Choose yours and we will tell you the part that actually matters before you fill anything in.

cheaper.title: I need cheaper insurance
bodies: The most common reason people call us. We put your details in front of every carrier we represent at once and show you what each one came back with, rather than defending a single company’s number.

Cheaper usually means a different company rather than less coverage. One form, several carriers, and the spread between them in front of you — that spread is the entire reason an independent agency exists.
Before cutting coverage, it is worth finding out what somebody else would charge for the same coverage. We shop it across the companies we represent and you see all of the answers, not one.

renewal.title: My renewal went up
bodies: Renewal increases often have nothing to do with you — carriers re-rate whole segments at once. It is worth finding out whether your carrier still wants your business before you simply pay the new number.
A renewal is a price your current company picked without competition. Re-shopping it is the only way to know whether the increase reflects the market or just that company’s appetite changing.
Nothing about your record has to change for a renewal to move. If yours jumped, the useful question is not why — it is what everyone else would charge you today.
renewal.cta: Check what else is out there

sr22.title: I need an SR-22
bodies: An SR-22 is not insurance. It is a form your insurer files with the state to confirm you carry the required liability coverage. Not every carrier files them, which is exactly why shopping matters here.

The SR-22 itself is paperwork — a filing your insurance company makes on your behalf. The part that matters is finding a carrier that both writes your policy and files the form, and they are not all willing.

bought.title: I just bought a car
bodies: Need coverage before you leave the dealership? Tell us the vehicle and we will compare available options from the companies we represent. Have the VIN handy if you can — it makes the quote far more accurate.

Buying is the moment worth re-shopping everything, not just adding the new car to the old policy. The vehicle changed, so the rating changed, and the company that was cheapest for the last one may not be for this one.

noprior.title: I don’t have prior insurance
bodies: A gap in coverage does make a quote harder, and it does not make it impossible. Carriers differ a lot in how they treat a lapse, so this is a case where seeing several at once is worth more than usual.

Some companies treat a lapse as disqualifying and some barely blink. Since you cannot tell which is which from the outside, putting the same details to all of them at once is the only sensible approach.

newdriver.title: I’m a new driver
bodies: A first policy, or a young driver being added to a household one. Which carrier is reasonable about it varies more than people expect, and so does whether a good-student discount applies.
First policies are where the spread between companies is widest, because there is no record to rate on yet. Ask about the good-student discount — it is real, and nobody applies it for you.

switch.title: I want to switch companies
bodies: You can change carriers mid-term — you are usually refunded the unused part of what you paid. The thing to avoid is a gap between the two policies, and we will make sure there is not one.
Switching does not have to wait for renewal. The one rule is that the new policy starts before the old one ends — a gap of even a few days follows you into future quotes.

mexico.title: I drive into Mexico
bodies: A U.S. auto policy generally does not provide the liability coverage Mexico requires. Driving south of the border usually means a separate Mexican policy for the days you are there. Ask us before the trip, not after.

Your U.S. policy and driving legally in Mexico are two different things. A separate Mexican auto policy is the normal answer, bought for the days you will be down there. It takes minutes to arrange in advance and cannot be fixed afterwards.

commercial.title: I use my vehicle for work
bodies: Carrying tools or materials for pay, towing for money, delivery, or a vehicle titled to a business — a personal auto policy can deny a claim that happened while working. Tell us what it actually does.
The question is not what the vehicle is, it is what it does. Hauling your own things is one thing; hauling anyone else’s for money is another, and so is a truck registered to a company.

factors.h2: Driving in {city} has a few local twists.
factors.lede: None of these are unique to insurance, and all of them come up when we quote drivers here.

h2: What comes up when we quote drivers in {city}
The {city} details worth knowing before you quote
road:
Getting around {city}

Traffic here runs on {road}, and how much of it you sit in is one of the few things on a quote form you control. Annual mileage and the address the car is parked at overnight both move the price, and both are worth getting right rather than estimating high.

We write across {county} County, so if you moved within it recently that is worth a call — a change of address can change the premium even when nothing else did.

{city} roads, and what they cost you

With {road} carrying the traffic, a commute here can look very different from one a few miles away, and carriers price that difference. Mileage is one of the questions where guessing high quietly costs money every month.

A move inside {county} County counts as a change too. Tell us and we will re-run it; sometimes it goes the right way.

Where you drive in {city}

Most local driving comes back to {road}. How far you go and where the car sits at night are both rating factors, which is why two neighbors with the same car and the same record can be quoted differently.

If anything has changed — a new job, a shorter commute, a move within {county} County — it is worth re-shopping rather than letting the renewal carry the old assumption.
border:
Driving both sides of the river

A Mexican policy does not cover you north of the bridge, and a US policy does not cover you south of it. People in {city} get caught by that in both directions — usually after the accident, not before. If you cross regularly, say so; some carriers handle it cleanly and some will not touch it.

A foreign license, a matrícula consular or a passport is not the dead end a call center will tell you it is. We are appointed with carriers that write those drivers every day, and having been turned down somewhere else does not count for much here.

Crossing, and what your policy does when you do

Coverage stops at the border in both directions. The US policy on your car does nothing once you are south of the bridge, and Mexican coverage does nothing once you are back in {city}. Most people learn which is which at the worst possible moment.

Being licensed abroad is not a reason to be refused. Foreign licenses, matrículas and passports are ordinary here, and we place drivers on them regularly — a no from one company is a statement about that company, not about you.

What the bridge does to your coverage

Two policies, two countries, no overlap. If you drive across from {city} with only a US policy you are uninsured the moment you cross, and Mexican coverage does not follow you home either. Tell your agent how often you cross — it changes which carriers make sense.

We also write plenty of drivers on a foreign license or a matrícula consular. It narrows the shelf; it does not close it.
rgv:
What the Valley costs you

Rates across the Rio Grande Valley are shaped by two things that have nothing to do with how you drive: uninsured motorists and hail. Both are priced into every quote you will see in {city}, and both are exactly why comparing carriers matters more here than in a quiet suburb — companies disagree sharply about what to charge for them.

Two things every Valley quote is really pricing

Uninsured drivers and hail. Neither is about your record, both land in your premium, and carriers put wildly different numbers on them. That spread is the reason a single quote tells you almost nothing about what insurance in {city} should cost — and the reason shopping the whole shelf is worth the ten minutes.

Why {city} quotes come back so far apart

Two risks dominate rating in the Valley: how many drivers around you are uninsured, and how often hail comes through. Companies assess both very differently, so the gap between the cheapest and dearest quote here is usually wider than people expect. Worth seeing all of them before you renew.
oil:
Work trucks and highway miles

Around {city} a lot of vehicles are not commuters — they are trucks running to a site and back, sometimes on a company's business and sometimes on yours. That distinction decides which policy you need, and getting it wrong is how a claim gets denied. If the truck in your driveway does any work, say so and we will quote it properly.

Long highway mileage moves the price too. Annual miles is one of the few questions where the honest answer usually helps you.

If the truck works, the policy has to know

Personal auto and commercial auto are different products, and in {city} the line between them runs through a lot of driveways. A truck used for a job, hauling for pay, or carrying tools to a site may not be covered by a personal policy — and that is found out at claim time, which is too late.

Tell us what the vehicle actually does. It takes a minute and it is the difference between a paid claim and a denied one.

Miles, trucks and the questions worth answering honestly

Two things set {city} apart on a rate sheet: the mileage people put on a vehicle, and how many of those vehicles are working trucks rather than commuters. Both change the policy you should be on. Understating either looks cheaper on the quote and costs more at the claim.
coastal:
Wind, water and what auto insurance will not do

On the coast the thing people get wrong is which policy pays. Comprehensive on your auto policy covers a flooded car; your homeowners policy does not cover a flooded house — that is separate flood coverage, and it usually has a waiting period. If you are in {city} carrying liability only, hurricane season is an expensive time to find that out.

Which policy pays when the water comes

A flooded car is an auto claim, and only if you carry comprehensive. A flooded house is not a homeowners claim at all — flood is its own policy, bought separately, and it does not start the day you buy it. Both catch people out in {city} every season, and both are cheap to fix in advance.

Liability only, on the coast

Liability pays for the damage you do to someone else. It does not pay for your own car — not in a wreck, and not when water reaches the floorboards. In {city} that gap is worth pricing out before the forecast makes the decision for you.
metro:
Why the ZIP code matters as much as the driver

Carriers rate {city} by garaging address, and the difference between two neighbourhoods a few miles apart is real money. Claim frequency, theft, repair costs and how far you commute all feed the number — which is also why one company can be cheapest for your block and a different one cheapest for your cousin's.

Same city, different price

Where the car sleeps matters as much as who drives it. In a market the size of {city} carriers price by garaging address, and two households with identical records on opposite sides of town can be quoted very differently. There is no way to know which company likes your address except to ask all of them.

What actually moves the number here

Your record is only part of it. In {city} a quote is built from the address the car is kept at, the miles you put on it and what it costs to repair — and carriers weigh those differently enough that the cheapest company changes from one neighbourhood to the next.
plains:
Hail is the claim out here

Roofs and hoods take a beating, and comprehensive — not collision — is the coverage that pays for it. Carriers price hail very differently county by county, so a quote from a single company tells you almost nothing about what {city} should actually cost you.

The coverage most people find out about too late

Around {city} the claim that shows up is weather, not a wreck, and it is comprehensive that pays for it. Drivers who cut comprehensive to save a few dollars a month discover the trade the first spring a storm comes through — and by then it is not a decision any more.

Storm country pricing

Hail frequency is one of the biggest rating factors in this part of the state, and it is one where companies disagree most. Two carriers looking at the same {city} address, the same car and the same clean record can be hundreds apart for that reason alone.
mountain:
High desert driving

Sun glare, blowing dust and a hard freeze a few nights a year are the local hazards around {city}, and none of them show up on a rate table. What does show up is your claim history — which is why the cheapest carrier for a clean record here is often not the cheapest one for a driver with a recent claim.

What the altitude does not change

Dust storms and glare make for real hazards around {city}, but carriers do not rate weather the way drivers assume. What they rate is the claim record it produces, yours and your neighbors'. That is why shopping matters most for the people who have actually had a claim.

Driving around {city}

Long dry stretches, sudden dust and a handful of hard freezes are the conditions here. None of them appear on a quote form — but the claims they cause do appear in what every carrier charges, and they do not all read that history the same way.
university:
Students, and the discount nobody claims

Adding a student to the policy is usually the single largest jump a household sees. Good-student and student-away-at-school discounts exist at most carriers and are routinely missed, because nobody asks. In {city} it is worth asking every renewal, not once.

The cheapest question a parent can ask

Is the student on the policy getting the good-student discount, and if they are away at school without a car, is that on file? Both are standard at most carriers, both are worth real money, and both are missed constantly because they are opt-in. Ask us in {city} and we will check every carrier we quote.

Young drivers here

A new driver is the biggest single change most {city} households make to a policy, and carriers vary enormously in how hard they price it. That variance is the opportunity: the company that was cheapest for you alone is frequently not the cheapest one once a teenager is on it.
military:
If you are stationed here

Military households in {city} have two questions civilians do not: which state the vehicle is registered in, and what happens to the policy during a deployment. Both have answers that save money, and both are easier to get right before a move than after.

Orders, registration and the policy

Where a car is registered and where it is garaged can be two different states for a service member in {city}, and that combination is priced differently by every carrier. A deployment changes it again. Tell us the situation rather than the simplified version — the simplified version usually costs more.

Coverage that follows a posting

Stationed at or near {city}? Storage during a deployment, an out-of-state registration and a spouse driving in the meantime are all ordinary requests, and carriers answer them very differently. Sorting it out in advance is cheaper than sorting it out from somewhere else.
spanish:
En español, con una persona

Atendemos en español en {city} — no con un traductor ni con un menú de opciones, sino con un agente con licencia que le explica el deducible, el SR-22 o la cobertura de responsabilidad civil en el idioma en que usted quiere hacer la pregunta. Llámenos al 915-503-1207 o mande un mensaje al 915-594-3777.

Le atendemos en español

La mitad de nuestras conversaciones empiezan en español, y se nota la diferencia entre un agente que lo habla y uno que lo traduce. En {city} puede preguntar lo que sea — qué cubre, qué no, por qué subió el precio — y le contesta una persona con licencia. Llame al 915-503-1207 o escriba al 915-594-3777.

Sin barrera de idioma

Si prefiere hacer todo esto en español, en {city} no tiene que conformarse con un formulario traducido. Un agente con licencia le explica su póliza, sus opciones y lo que firma, en español y sin prisa. 915-503-1207 · 915-594-3777.

note: The legal floor in {state} is {short}. It is a floor written into law, not a recommendation from anybody — and the third number is what it would pay toward the other driver’s vehicle, which is worth comparing against what vehicles actually cost to replace.

Everyone in {state} has seen {short} written somewhere and very few have been told what it means. Injury to one person, injury to everyone in the accident, then damage to property — in that order, in thousands of dollars.

{state} will let you drive on {short}. That figure is set by statute rather than by anything to do with what a hospital stay or a replacement vehicle costs today, which is the whole reason it is worth looking at what sits above it.

cost:
Anyone quoting one figure for a whole city is guessing. Two households on the same street pay very differently depending on the vehicle, the record, the mileage and who else is on the policy — and carriers disagree with each other on all four.

What we can tell you is the spread. Running a quote in {city} through every carrier we represent, the gap between cheapest and dearest is routinely wide enough to matter. That is the number worth finding, and it takes a few minutes.

There is no average that helps you. A city-wide figure mixes a 19-year-old on a financed truck with a retiree on a paid-off sedan, and your quote will look like neither of them.

The number that matters is the range across carriers for your details, in {city}, today. We can have it back to you in a few minutes, and it costs nothing to find out.
cheapest:
No company is cheapest for everyone here, and any page that names one is selling you something. The cheapest carrier for a 45-year-old with a clean record and a paid-off sedan is frequently not the cheapest for a 22-year-old with a financed truck, or for a household with a recent claim.

The only honest answer is the one you get by asking all of them at once, which is what an independent agency is for.

It changes by driver, which is why the question does not have a fixed answer. Carriers each have an appetite — one wants clean records and newer cars, another is comfortable with a violation or a lapse — and the winner in {city} swaps depending on which of those you are.

We shop the whole shelf rather than defending one company's number, which is the difference between an agency and a carrier.
best:
Best depends on what you are optimising for. Cheapest today is not the same as best at paying a claim, and neither is the same as the one that will still want your business after an accident.

We are appointed with a shelf of carriers rather than employed by one, so we can tell you which is genuinely good for your situation instead of defending a single answer.

Three different questions hide inside that one: who is cheapest, who handles a claim well, and who will keep you after you file one. They rarely have the same answer.

Tell us which matters most to you and we will say so plainly — including when the cheapest quote on the screen is not the one we would put our own family on.
expensive:
Most of it is not about you. Premiums in any area are pushed up by how often claims are filed nearby, how many drivers around you are uninsured, what repairs cost locally, and weather. None of that is in your control, and all of it lands in your quote.

What you do control: your deductible, your mileage estimate, keeping coverage continuous, and whether every discount you qualify for is actually applied. That last one is missed more than anything else, because most discounts are opt-in.

Your premium is partly your record and largely your surroundings — local claim frequency, uninsured drivers, repair costs, theft and weather. That is why a spotless driver can still be quoted more in one place than another.

The lever that actually works is comparison. Carriers weigh those local risks very differently, so the same clean record in {city} can be priced hundreds apart depending on who is looking at it.
zip:
Yes — carriers rate on the address where the car is parked overnight, not on the city. Two addresses a few miles apart in {city} can be quoted differently on identical drivers and identical cars.

It also means a move is a reason to re-shop, even a short one. The company that was cheapest at your old address is not automatically cheapest at the new one.

It does, and more than most people expect. The garaging address — where the vehicle sits overnight — feeds theft rates, claim frequency and repair costs into the quote, and those vary block to block, not just city to city.

If you have moved within {city} recently and simply let the policy renew, that is worth ten minutes of our time and possibly some of your money.
minimum:
{state} requires at least {min}: {person} for injury to one person, {accident} per accident, and {property} for property damage.

That is what makes you legal. It is not what makes you covered — it pays nothing toward your own vehicle, and {property} does not replace a late-model truck. Before you decide, run it against your own numbers.

The legal floor is {min} in liability — {person} per injured person, {accident} per accident, {property} for the property you damage.

Read those numbers against what is actually on the road. {property} is the whole budget for someone else's vehicle, and none of the three does anything for yours. Run the numbers with your own figures.
lower:
Roughly in order of how much they move the number: shop it across carriers instead of renewing, raise your deductible to a figure you could genuinely cover tomorrow, correct an inflated mileage estimate, bundle if you have a home or renters policy, and make sure every discount is actually on the policy.

Do not lower it by dropping to the state minimum without doing the arithmetic. That is not saving money, it is moving risk onto yourself.

The biggest single win is usually the least exciting one: getting the same coverage quoted by every carrier rather than letting it renew. After that — a deductible you can actually afford, an honest mileage figure, bundling, and auditing the discounts.

What we would not do is cut liability to the legal minimum to hit a number. Work out first what that trade would really cost you.
full:
“Full coverage” is not a real product — it is shorthand for liability plus collision plus comprehensive. If your car is financed or leased, the lender requires the last two. If it is paid off, it is a judgement call.

The rough test: if writing a cheque for the car's full value tomorrow would not seriously hurt, liability-only can make sense. If it would, it does not.

There is no policy called full coverage. What people mean is liability plus collision plus comprehensive — the two that pay for your car. A lienholder will insist on them; once the car is yours outright, it becomes a decision.

Ask it this way: if the car were gone tomorrow, could you replace it out of pocket without it hurting? That answer is the coverage answer.
foreign:
Yes. A foreign license, a matrícula consular or a passport is workable — it narrows which carriers will write you, it does not rule them out. We place drivers on those documents regularly in {city}.

Being turned down by one company tells you about that company's appetite, not about whether you can be insured.

It is an ordinary situation here, not an obstacle. Some carriers write drivers on a foreign license or a matrícula without blinking and some will not touch it — knowing which is which is most of what an agency is for.

If you have already been refused somewhere, bring that with you. It changes nothing about where else you can be placed.

A city built around freight

Laredo is one of the busiest commercial land ports in the country, and a lot of households here have a vehicle that does something for work. If yours carries tools or materials for pay, tows for money, or is titled to a company, a personal auto policy can deny a claim that happened on the job.
I-35 starts here, and Loop 20 carries the rest

Between the interstate, the loop and US 83 along the river, a lot of everyday driving in Laredo happens at highway speed. Annual mileage is something a carrier asks about, and it is the figure people most often estimate from memory.
En español, con una persona
Nuestros agentes trabajan en español por teléfono o por mensaje. Los términos de cobertura son donde está la confusión, y vale la pena entenderlos en el idioma en que uno piensa.
faq: Does my Texas insurance cover me in Nuevo Laredo?

Generally not in the way you need. A standard U.S. auto policy does not usually satisfy Mexico’s liability requirements, and physical damage coverage commonly stops at the border. Most people crossing here buy a separate Mexican auto policy covering the days they will be over.

It takes minutes to arrange in advance and nothing can be done about it afterwards, which is the whole reason to ask before the trip rather than after.
¿Puedo hacer todo esto en español?

faq: I just moved to Texas. What do I need to do about my car insurance?

Two things. Your policy has to be rated on your new Texas garaging address, and Texas has its own minimum liability limits — 30/60/25 — which may not match what you carried before. Keeping the out-of-state policy indefinitely is not an option.

The useful part is that moving is a natural moment to re-shop rather than transfer. Your prior insurance history counts in your favour with most carriers, so bring the details of the old policy and we will put it to several companies at once.

faq: What is the minimum car insurance required in New Mexico?

New Mexico requires liability limits of 25/50/10 — $25,000 for injury to one person, $50,000 for everyone injured in one accident, and $10,000 for property damage.

The property damage figure is the one worth looking at twice. $10,000 is well below what a good many vehicles on the road are worth, and anything above that limit is yours to cover. A New Mexico insurer also has to offer you uninsured motorist coverage, which you can decline only in writing.

Flood and water damage is a comprehensive question

This is the one worth being precise about. A standard auto policy does not automatically cover flood damage to a vehicle — that generally falls under comprehensive coverage, which is optional, subject to your deductible, and subject to the terms of the policy you actually hold. Liability alone will not do it, and neither will collision. If your vehicle is paid off and you dropped comprehensive to save money, that is the coverage you no longer have.
Comprehensive covers more than weather

The same coverage answers hail, a tree limb, theft, a break-in and a cracked windshield. It is usually the cheaper half of physical damage cover and it is the half people drop first, which tends to be backwards.
Where the vehicle actually sits

A garage, a driveway, a carport, an apartment lot or the street — carriers ask, and in a metro this size the answer varies enormously between two households a mile apart. It is rated on the overnight address, not the one on your license.
Work vehicles around the Ship Channel

Houston has an unusual amount of vehicles doing something commercial — contractors, delivery, anything moving materials for pay. A personal auto policy can deny a claim that happened while working, so it is worth saying out loud what the vehicle does.
English or Spanish

Our agents work in both, by phone or text. Coverage terms are where the confusion usually is, and comprehensive versus collision is exactly the sort of thing worth going through in whichever language you think in.
faq: Does car insurance cover flood damage in Houston?

Not automatically, and not under liability or collision. Flood and water damage to a vehicle generally falls under comprehensive coverage, which is optional on a policy, applies subject to your deductible, and is governed by the terms and exclusions of the policy you actually hold.

The practical version: if you carry liability only, a flooded vehicle is your loss. If you carry comprehensive, it is a claim. It is worth checking which of those describes your policy before hurricane season rather than during it — we can look at your current declarations page with you.
Is comprehensive coverage worth it in Houston?

It is the coverage that answers hail, flooding, theft, break-ins and a rock through the windshield, and it is usually the cheaper half of physical damage cover. Whether it is worth carrying comes down to what the vehicle is worth and whether you could replace it out of pocket — not to any claim we could make about the weather.

If the vehicle is financed or leased, the question is settled for you: the lender will require it.
I commute from Katy into town. Does that change my quote?

Annual mileage is one of the things carriers rate on, so a long daily commute is relevant — and so is the address the vehicle is parked at overnight, which for a lot of Houston households is nowhere near where they work.

Estimate the mileage honestly rather than optimistically. Guessing low is not a saving; it is a mismatch between the policy and the way the vehicle is actually used.

Comprehensive is the part of the policy that covers hail, flooding, theft and a cracked windshield — not collision, and not liability. It is subject to your deductible and to the terms of the policy, and it is the coverage most often dropped by people who then need it.
faq: Does my Texas auto insurance cover me when I drive into Mexico?

Generally not in the way you need it to. A standard U.S. auto policy does not usually satisfy Mexico’s liability requirements, and physical damage coverage often stops at the border as well. Most people crossing at the Juárez bridges buy a separate Mexican auto policy for the days they will be there.

Ask us before you go. It is quick to arrange and it is not something you want to discover at the border or, worse, after an accident.
Can Safe House help me in Spanish?

Yes — on the phone, by text, and in person at the office on Montana Ave. Se habla español.

That includes going through the policy itself rather than just the price. Coverage terms are where the confusion usually is, and they are worth understanding in whichever language you think in.
